pitch.short: I spent two years planning supply for Pinewick Paper & Print in Larchmont Falls and one spring in a Marlowe Heights pick room. I put a stopwatch on the work before I trust the spreadsheet.
why_hire: Two years in supply planning at Pinewick Paper & Print: line balancing, two-bin replenishment and supplier follow-up for a regional paper and stationery maker.
I rebalanced the poster finishing line for a new framed range and cut the bottleneck station from 172 s to 142 s, under the 150 s takt, without hiring anyone.
At Tallgrass Office Wholesale I re-slotted 280 fast-moving SKUs in a pilot pick room and the average pick dropped from 2 min 34 s to 2 min 03 s.

about.intro: I grew up in Larchmont Falls, where the river drops forty feet and the paper mill still sets the shift whistle. I studied industrial and production engineering at Brackenridge Institute of Technology. In 2023 I joined Pinewick Paper & Print as a graduate supply trainee under Gordon 'Gordie' Pruitt, the regional manager, and spent two years in supply planning: balancing the finishing line, running replenishment for small consumables and chasing suppliers when pallets were late at the dock. In 2025 I started a PGP at Marlowe School of Management to see supply chains beyond one plant, and in spring 2026 I spent ten weeks on pick-room operations at Tallgrass Office Wholesale.
about.now: Adding supplier lead times to a reorder sheet for the Pinewick front desk, writing Ream Counts every second Sunday and planning an autumn walk along the Birchlands ridge.

projects.title: Rebalancing the poster finishing line for a new framed range

projects.result: Bottleneck station from 172 s to 142 s; Saturday overtime stopped within six weeks

projects.title: Two-bin replenishment and a weekly OTIF review for 12 suppliers

trim-line-balance.context: The Mill Lane finishing line turns printed posters into framed, boxed cartons through eleven stations against a takt time of 150 seconds. In August 2024 Gordie's new framed 'Rise & Grind' range, with a gloss lamination and a corner-fitted frame, entered the mix at roughly a third of output.
trim-line-balance.problem: Stations 3, 4 and 7 each took on about 35 extra seconds. Station 3 hit 172 s on framed cartons, the shift plan fell 60 to 80 cartons short daily, and Saturday overtime ran for five weeks in a row, which Gordie called 'a growth opportunity' on the whiteboard.
trim-line-balance.my_role: Supply Planning Analyst, led the rebalance
what_i_did: Stopwatched each task across all eleven stations on three shifts, with a line lead from every shift beside me, 34 framed cartons in total.

Turned the time study into a yamazumi chart in Python, so everyone could see where framed-range work stacked up. Dennis Hale checked the sheet and asked only that I stop rounding to a tenth of a second.
Shifted six tasks, among them lamination from station 3 to the quiet station 5, once each had passed a sequence and tool-reach check.
Tested the new balance on a single shift for a fortnight with the line leads, and only then edited the standard work sheets.
Updated the ERP routing and the operator cards for the moved tasks.

decisions.choice: Move tasks, not add an operator
decisions.why: Hiring would have added a whole salary for a range that was a third of output, while station 5 sat idle for 38 s on every carton.
The other two shifts stayed on the old sequence until the first had settled tool placement, and Wendell Odom's crew had time to adjust pallet staging.

results.note: of shifts the following quarter, from 70% before

trim-line-balance.learned: The line leads could have told me where the minutes were going without the stopwatch. Measuring beside them, rather than behind their backs, is what made the moves hold on all three shifts.
trim-line-balance.next: Add the product mix to the monthly balance check so Gordie's next range is planned before its launch poster is printed.

pick-room-routing.context: Tallgrass Office Wholesale's Marlowe Heights fulfilment room holds about 3,500 SKUs on a floor of around 3,000 sq ft and aims to pick and pack a standard order in under three minutes. Stock was shelved in catalogue order, the way the printed price list reads.
pick-room-routing.problem: In the afternoon peak the pilot room's average pick time was 2 min 34 s. Pickers crossed the room several times for small baskets because copier paper, pens and envelopes sat at opposite ends.
what_i_did: Followed pickers through six shifts and timed 380 picks, each split into walk, search and scan.
Took three weeks of order lines and drew a pick heat map by bin with Python.
Re-slotted the 280 fastest-moving SKUs (about 58% of picks) into a zone beside the packing bench.
Re-sorted the pick list into a single S-shaped walk, leaving heavy goods until the end.
Piloted it for three weeks next to a matched control room, with a daily dashboard for the room manager.

decisions.choice: Re-slot 280 SKUs, not the whole room
decisions.why: The night team could move about 95 SKUs a night without missing replenishment. 280 SKUs covered most of the walking.
Boxes of paper stay at the bottom of the tote and nothing gets crushed. Pickers already did this out of habit.
Order volumes swing with school terms and quarter-end budgets, so a before-and-after in one room would have misled us.

results.note: the new layout did not raise errors

pick-room-routing.learned: New pickers lost more time hunting than walking, so legible bin numbers proved as valuable as the move itself. A third of the crew was under a month in.
pick-room-routing.next: Repeat the slotting every month from fresh order data, and try the layout in a second room with a different floor plan.

school-delivery-routes.context: The client is the Birchlands Schools Supply Co-op, which delivers paper, toner and stationery twice a week to 46 school drop points from 6 depots across the district. Cartons are meant to reach the school office before the caretaker locks up at 3:30 pm.
school-delivery-routes.problem: In October and November 3.1% of cartons were refused, rained on or left on a step overnight. On the two longest rounds it was 3.4%, and schools on those rounds were quietly buying from the stationery shop in town instead.
what_i_did: Rode four delivery rounds from 6 am and logged arrival time and weather at every school.
Mapped all 46 drop points and 6 depots in QGIS with road distances and caretaker lock-up times.
Re-sequenced the two longest rounds so the schools with the earliest lock-up come first and the van finishes at the nearest depot.
Costed a seventh, smaller depot for the longest rounds and worked out the payback in a spreadsheet with the co-op's logistics head.
Trialled the new order on two rounds for a fortnight ahead of the final presentation.

decisions.choice: Change the round order before opening a depot
decisions.why: A new round order was free and could be trialled within a week, whereas a depot needed board sign-off.

decisions.choice: Measure arrival time, not just distance
decisions.why: Two short rounds scored worst because the van sat at a school gate while someone looked for the delivery form.

results.note: mean of the two pilot rounds

school-delivery-routes.learned: The biggest delay was waiting at the gate, not driving. A promised arrival window that school offices trusted beat any shortcut on the map.
school-delivery-routes.next: The co-op has put the seventh depot into next year's budget. I would add a cheap GPS tag to each van before then.

values: Put a stopwatch on the work before you redraw the plan.
Fix the process alongside the people who run it, starting with whoever knows where the pallets really are.
Try each change on one shift, one room or one route before announcing it.
